title: Chimaji Appa Opens Vasai's Gates
subtitle: How Chimaji Appa Loosened the Konkan from the Empire of the Cross
region: Thane, Salsette, Arnala, Tarapur and Vasai on the Konkan coast
moral: Patient preparation can break the strongest wall.

sources.citation: Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Lisbon, Portuguese records of the Vasai campaign
sources.note: Primary Portuguese accounts for the siege and loss of Bassein.

sources.citation: Chimaji Appa's Modi-script letter to Nanasaheb Peshwa on the campaign
sources.note: Maratha-side primary correspondence preserved in Deccan archives.
Modern context for the campaign's revenue and coastal consequences.

dialogue.text: In the year of 1739, Chimaji Appa faced the walls of Vasai—and with patience, gunpowder and sea-wind, broke the oldest foreign stronghold on the northern Konkan.
For two centuries the Portuguese Estado watched the Konkan creeks. From Bassein they held harbours, customs houses and churches, and their cannons kept the Arabian Sea lanes in their grip.
After the ruin of the Peshwa at Delhi, the Deccan needed coin, coast and confidence. Chimaji Appa turned to the sea, knowing that as long as Bassein stood, Maratha power ended at the surf.
Modern scholars read his letters and ledgers and see the hidden war—bullock trains, gunfounders, rice convoys and sailors. Before he spoke of glory, Chimaji Appa moved food, metal and men.

panels.shot: dramatic long shot of first assault

dialogue.text: He did not dash at Bassein. He began at Arnala in 1737, feeling the tides, testing Portuguese fire, learning how to carry war by boat to an island crown of stone.
When Arnala fell, a small island changed hands. Yet in Goa and Lisbon, reports began speaking of a new Maratha art—of siege lines, trenches and heavy guns instead of only swift horsemen.

Step by careful step he walked up the coast. Thane and Salsette, Dahanu and Mahim—each fort cut away, each creek closed—until Bassein, once encircled by Portuguese allies, stood like a lone tree in a cleared field.
Bassein was no hill stronghold. It was a walled city with magazines, churches, storehouses and a harbour, planned for long sieges. Portuguese records called it ‘the bulwark of the north’.

dialogue.speaker: chimaji_appa
dialogue.text: We shall not dash ourselves on their walls. We will walk the earth closer, day by day.

The Marathas studied European manuals taken in earlier wars, and matched them with Deccan earth-work. Saps crept forward, trenches snake-like, so that cannon and men could approach without being shredded.

Portuguese chronicles speak of ‘furious bombardment’. Yet fury rested on supply—powder hauled from inland towns, iron balls cast in coastal workshops, guns dragged through monsoon slush and mounted on muddy batteries.
In a letter to the Peshwa, his pen moved between devotion and detail. He reported batteries raised, breaches widening, food stockpiles guarded, and the slow tightening of the ring around the city.

panels.shot: medium shot of dealing with setbacks

dialogue.text: Portuguese counter-fire wrecked guns and platforms, and sorties harassed the trenches. Recent studies show how often he shifted batteries, adjusted range and rebuilt, seeking angles where enemy cannon could not answer.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of breach in wall

dialogue.text: Week after week the same rhythm—dig, drag, fire, withdraw. On a May morning in 1739, a section of the wall finally sagged. The breach was not only in stone; the spirit inside had begun to crack.

Portuguese records speak of councils filled with fear. Supplies dwindled, relief from the sea did not come, and the outer works lay in Maratha hands. Representatives came to talk, weighing surrender against honour and ruin.

dialogue.speaker: chimaji_appa
dialogue.text: Your king’s writ will end at these walls. Your people will live if they accept this truth.

On 16 May 1739, after months of attrition, the gates opened. No sudden storming, no romantic melee—only exhausted men walking out and a patient besieger riding in to claim the most prized harbour of the north.

He found magazines, shipyards and storehouses built over generations. The Maratha treasury gained not only artillery and coin, but customs over creeks, rights over fields and control of a stitched web of coastal trade.
From Goa southwards the Portuguese still ruled, but north of it the pattern had changed. The loss of Bassein broke their coastal chain and shifted harbours, fields and ferries into Maratha hands.

Later ages wrapped his name in legend and bells, but the records show something quieter—an inland warrior who learned to fight the sea-walled city, and who taught his people that patience, powder and planning could unmake an empire.
